nameStory: The regal jumping spider earned its royal title from its impressive size and commanding presence - it's the largest jumping spider in eastern North America! Like a tiny monarch of the spider world, it carries itself with confidence, often boldly approaching curious observers rather than fleeing. The name 'regal' perfectly captures this spider's dignified bearing and striking appearance.
description: The regal jumping spider is a robust, chunky arachnid that's built more like a tiny tank than the delicate spiders many people picture. These impressive hunters can grow quite large for jumping spiders, with females reaching particularly substantial sizes. Their bodies are covered in dense, velvety hairs that give them an almost fuzzy appearance, and they move with deliberate, confident movements rather than the skittery motions of many other spiders. Unlike web-building spiders, these are active hunters that stalk their prey with cat-like precision.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Noticeably larger and more robust than other jumping spiders - females especially feel substantial and chunky when observed, with a body that looks almost barrel-shaped

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Stocky, compact build with a broad, rounded abdomen covered in dense, soft-looking hairs that give it a velvety texture

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large front-facing eyes arranged in a distinctive pattern, with the two center eyes noticeably larger and giving it an almost mammal-like gaze

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Remarkably bold and curious, often turning to face observers directly and approaching rather than fleeing - moves with slow, deliberate stalking motions

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Variable coloring often includes iridescent patches that shimmer green or blue in sunlight, with distinctive white or light-colored markings on the face and body

habitat: Regal jumping spiders are extremely rare visitors to New England, far outside their typical range in the southeastern United States. The single observation likely represents an accidental introduction, perhaps arriving on shipped goods or plants from warmer climates. In their native habitat, they prefer warm, sunny areas with plenty of vegetation and hunting opportunities.

seasonality.spring: Any spring sighting in New England would be extraordinary and likely represents an accidental introduction that probably won't survive the climate.
seasonality.summer: The warmest months would offer the best chance for survival if accidentally introduced, when they might be found sunning themselves on warm surfaces.
seasonality.fall: Unlikely to survive New England's cooling temperatures, as these are warm-climate spiders adapted to southern conditions.
seasonality.winter: Cannot survive New England winters outdoors, though might persist briefly in heated greenhouses or indoor spaces.

funFact: Regal jumping spiders are so confident and curious that they'll actually turn to watch you watching them, often tilting their heads like tiny dogs trying to figure out what you are - some people have even trained them to jump to their hands on command!
confusionNotes: In the extremely unlikely event you spot one in New England, you might confuse it with the much more common Bold Jumping Spider, but regals are noticeably larger and chunkier - think 'heavyweight boxer' versus 'lightweight fighter' in terms of build.
contextualKnowledge: This species is included mainly for completeness, as it's essentially a tropical tourist in New England. The single recorded observation likely represents an accidental stowaway rather than an established population, so don't expect to find one in your garden!
compareHints: Compared to its common New England cousin the Bold Jumping Spider, the regal is significantly larger and more robust with a chunkier build. While Bold Jumping Spiders have crisp black and white patterns, regals often show more variable coloring with iridescent highlights. The regal's size alone - nearly twice as large as a bold jumper - makes it distinctive among the Phidippus genus in our region.
